title: Enterprise SLA Playbook for Dedicated Inference
summary: Working playbook for commercial and technical conversations when selling Dedicated capacity to enterprise buyers. Emphasizes measurable SLAs, network/data isolation, predictable throughput guarantees, and procurement-friendly contract language. Draft is intended for AE and solutions engineering use during procurement cycles; not final legal text.
audience: Enterprise platform architects, procurement teams, cloud infra leads, SRE managers, sales AEs, solutions engineers
objectives: 1) Give a repeatable framing for why customers should buy Dedicated capacity rather than hosted, 2) Provide quantifiable SLA and throughput language that maps to procurement checkpoints, 3) Supply crisp objection responses and configurable commercial levers (credits, penalties, onboarding milestones), 4) Reduce negotiation cycles by surfacing standard contract anchors.
positioning_statement: For enterprise engineering teams that need predictable inference economics and operational isolation, Redwood Dedicated combines cluster-level isolation, capacity commitments, and engineered fallbacks so production LLM features run within agreed latency and throughput envelopes — with observability and playbooks that map directly into procurement and SRE acceptance criteria.
value_props: Predictable per-minute throughput: contractable pool size with capacity reservation that maps to customer QPS and token budgets
SLA-backed latency windows (P95/P99) and availability commitments with credits on breach
Logical and physical isolation options (VPC peering, dedicated GPU pools, single-tenant options) to satisfy compliance and data residency needs
Operational runbook handed to customer: onboarding run, traffic shaping controls, configured fallback policies to hosted variants for graceful degradation
Transparent cost/usage reporting down to token-level and route-level to reconcile billing and capacity consumption
proof_points: Benchmarks vs. public clouds: consistent P99 < 400ms on text-generation workloads at 32 token contexts for reserved capacity (internal tests, Q4 2024)
Customer pilots: two fintech customers moved to Dedicated and reduced unexpected throttling incidents by 87% in first 90 days
Operational playbooks tested in multi-tenant to single-tenant migrations; typical onboarding to prod in 3–6 weeks with a standard integration checklist
procurement_checklist: Defined throughput requirement: tokens/sec or qps per route + expected burst profile
Requested SLOs: availability (%) and latency windows (P95/P99) per route
Isolation level: shared-dedicated pool vs. single-tenant vs. on-prem; networking (VPC, private link) and data plane residency
Audit & security controls: KMS/HSM integration, SIEM forwarding, access logs retention
Billing model: committed monthly GPU-hours/instances or committed token throughput + overage pricing
Operational handover milestones: staging sign-off, performance validation plan, rollback/fallback triggers
Penalty/credit mechanics: clear trigger for credit, cap on credits, remediation window
Support & escalation paths: 24/7 incident contacts, periodic SLA reviews, scheduled capacity planning syncs
sample_sla_snippets: Availability: 99.9% monthly uptime for Dedicated inference control plane; credits applied pro rata for eligible downtime
Latency: P95 <= 250ms, P99 <= 750ms for specified model family and context length under committed capacity; credit entitlement if sustained breach beyond 72 hours

Throughput: Customer reserved pool will sustain X tokens/sec (contract exhibit A). If capacity is exceeded, Redwood will (a) enable configured burst buffer for Y minutes and (b) route to fallback model only if configured by customer
Remediation: Redwood will provide a root cause analysis within 5 business days for incidents impacting contracted SLOs
commercial_levers_and_tradeoffs: Higher committed capacity reduces unit price and tightens latency targets — useful for high QPS customers
Add-on: priority capacity slices that are isolated from shared bursts for an additional fixed fee
Shorter onboarding timelines increase setup fees (accelerated ops engagement)
Longer contract terms (12/24/36 months) lower overage rates and allow for reserved hardware placement
objection_handling: "We can keep using hosted APIs and scale as needed" — Response: hosted is great for headroom and fast experiments; for production traffic with contractual SLAs and steady QPS, Dedicated removes noisy neighbors, makes cost predictable, and surfaces SRE-grade controls that procurement requires

"What about vendor lock-in?" — Response: Redwood Dedicated exposes standard APIs; rollback paths include model pinning and automated fallbacks to compatible hosted variants. Contract includes limited exit assistance (data exports + rollback latency profiles)

"How do we prove capacity before signing?" — Response: we offer a short proof-of-capacity pilot (two-week soak) with defined test harness and acceptance metrics; pilot deliverables become part of contract exhibits
competitive_notes: Generic cloud vendors: can offer similar hardware but lack inference-optimized runtime and built-in prefix/KV caching — leads to higher unit costs or unpredictable latency under mixed workloads
API-first LLM providers: strong on models and developer ergonomics but weaker on dedicated isolation and procurement-friendly capacity agreements

Self-hosted open-source stacks: control but high ops burden and slower time-to-value; Redwood reduces ops by shipping a runtime + orchestration layer and handles kernel selection and quantization profiles
Key differentiation to call out: turnkey reserved pool with observability and playbooks that map directly into procurement and SRE acceptance criteria
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: SLA metric disputes due to differing test harnesses — Mitigation: include standardized performance test harness (exhibit B) and mutually agreed traffic profiles
Risk: Unexpected model updates change latency profile — Mitigation: version pinning and canary rollout policy by default. Also include regression alerting tied to customer test prompts
Risk: Procurement expects deep discounts immediately — Mitigation: present staged commercial package: pilot discount, then ramped committed capacity with price breaks at defined bands
procurement_language_examples: Exhibit A: Reserved Capacity — Provider will reserve N GPU-hours and maintain a dedicated pool sufficient to sustain the committed throughput profile as defined in this exhibit

Exhibit B: Performance Validation — Prior to go-live, parties will execute the Performance Validation Plan; acceptance requires meeting P95/P99 and throughput thresholds for two consecutive 24-hour windows
Termination for Convenience: customer may terminate with 90 days' notice; termination charges limited to unused committed credits or a predefined early-exit fee
handoff_and_playbook_for_se: SE actions for discovery: capture peak tokens/sec, tail latency requirements per route, allowed fallback policies, compliance boundaries (data residency, VPC needs)
Pre-sign tech-deck: include sample latency vs. throughput curves for candidate model families under reserved pool
Post-sign ops run: schedule capacity reservation window, set up monitoring dashboards, run pilot soak test, document acceptance criteria and rollback plan
